tagline: A valley trail became a stagecoach road, then a marked history route
intro: Alabama’s Stagecoach Route Through Leeds travels north through a valley of horse farms, historic homes, churches and cemeteries. Alabama Byways lists it among the state byways and presents its historic sites and natural setting as the reasons to follow it. Including the Shelby County entry, the scenic byway extends approximately eighteen miles.

The route began as an Indian trail through a watershed. Andrew Jackson’s scouts widened it in 1812–13 while seeking roads for supply wagons. When European settlers entered the Leeds valley in 1820, the widened trail became a stagecoach route. The Leeds Historical Society marked the route in 1998; St. Clair County extended the marking in 2000 along the Ashville-to-Montevallo road to the Etowah County line. The society also documented homes, churches, businesses and cemeteries along the road. Alabama Byways reports more than twenty-two historical markers in Leeds and recognition for thirty sites.

Follow the valley north from the Lake Purdy area toward Leeds and Moody. In Leeds, signs on the 119/411 bridges identify the Little Cahaba River, and riverside parks have monuments and interpretive exhibits. The byway account describes a downtown district dating from the turn of the twentieth century. Beyond Leeds, U.S. 411 leads northeast to Moody.

moments.title: Little Cahaba River
moments.text: The river has its name on the road: signs on the 119/411 bridges in Leeds identify the Little Cahaba. The Leeds Historical Society obtained that recognition from the Alabama Department of Transportation. The parks beside the river carry local history into the landscape through monuments, flags and interpretive exhibits.
moments.notice: Look for the Little Cahaba River name on the 119/411 bridges.

moments.title: Leeds
moments.text: Leeds has grown beside a river, a stagecoach road and two railroads. Its incorporation came on April 27, 1887. The city’s name for itself, the City of Valor, honors three residents who received the Medal of Honor for service in World War II and the Korean War: Alford McLaughlin, William Lawley and Henry “Red” Erwin. Their names also belong to the road: the Alabama legislature designated the Erwin, Lawley & McLaughlin Medal of Honor Highway on 119 from I-65 through Leeds. A wall in the Jonathan Bass House Museum is dedicated to McLaughlin, Lawley and Erwin, bringing the three names together within the local history collection.

moments.title: John Henry's tunnel
moments.text: Leeds places a railroad tunnel at the center of its John Henry story. Alabama Byways reports that John Garst’s studies locate the legendary contest at the C&W Railroad’s Oak Tunnel in the 1880s. The same account says descendants of the original Black-American settlers agree with the claim that Henry was a real person who raced the steam drill in Leeds. It identifies these claims as local folklore. Folklorist John Garst has argued that the contest took place at either Coosa Mountain Tunnel or Oak Mountain Tunnel.
